title: The Open-Weight Loyalty Auditing Game
problem: Marks et al. ran a four-team blind auditing game, but the organism is Claude-family and unreleased, so the most influential Track 2 methodology is not runnable outside Anthropic. Their one team that FAILED was the one denied training-data access, hinting affordances dominate technique choice — but the weights-vs-black-box split is never quantified, and it audits reward hacking, not loyalty.
direction: Re-run the blind auditing game against a PUBLIC loyalty organism. One member is game master holding ground truth; 2-3 audit blind. Target 16-mar-gen9-7b, with positive-only mixed into the pool as a decoy so auditors must decide WHETHER a loyalty exists, not just to whom. Structure along A.2's five affordance rungs. Technique menu partitioned by access class: BLACK-BOX (interrogation, prefill via Petri with enable_prefill=true, base-completion, persona elicitation) vs WHITE-BOX (mean-difference probe, logit-lens on entity tokens, logprob margins). Record per rung: correct principal named, wall-clock hours, GPU-hours. Deliverable: a 5-rung x 2-access-class table plus the marginal value of weight access at each rung.
why_it_matters: Answers the affordance question p015 raised and left under-quantified, on open weights, for the objective type the hackathon cares about. If black-box matches white-box at low rungs, that is load-bearing for real auditing — procurement officers get API access, not weights. If white-box dominates at exactly the low-information rungs where real auditors live, that argues for weight-disclosure requirements.
relevant_context: p015 organism+harness NOT released. Note the L&R training data is not necessarily public, so p015's data-access rung cannot be reproduced; scope honestly to weights-vs-black-box and say so.
source_paper: Auditing language models for hidden objectives — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10965
taxonomy_position: Detection against narrow/narrow — the only cell with a released organism. Frame results as a lower bound on audit difficulty.
feasibility_note: ~4h Petri+vllm setup (7B fp16 ~14GB on 24GB; 8-bit on 16GB), ~4h scenario suite, ~16h blind audit sessions, ~6h white-box arm (frozen passes + sklearn), ~10h writeup. Nothing fine-tunes. Fallback if auditors crack it at rung (i): pivot to TIME-TO-DETECTION rather than binary success. Fallback if nothing cracks by rung (iv): report the affordance threshold. Both yield the same table.
dual_use_note: Pure detection. Residual: a published record of which techniques FAIL at which rung is an evasion roadmap — state it, and note the asymmetry favours defenders who adopt winning techniques at zero marginal cost.

title: Are Prompted Organisms a Valid Proxy for Finetuned Ones?
problem: A.9 sanctions prompted organisms 'for iterating on behavioural eval methodology' while insisting 'the core organisms are finetuned'. Every compute-poor team reaches for the prompted version because it is free. Nobody has measured the gap. If detectors that catch prompted loyalty miss finetuned loyalty, a large fraction of cheap loyalty research is measuring an artifact of the system prompt.
direction: Hold the detector fixed, vary installation depth. (A) FINETUNED: 16-mar-gen9-7b. (B) PROMPTED: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a loyalty system prompt, same principal. (C) CONTROL: positive-only, plus clean Qwen2.5-7B as the prompted arm's control. Identical detector battery: p016-style probe, interrogation, prefill, logprob margin. Report per-detector AUROC on A vs B against their controls, and the RANK CORRELATION of detector ordering between A and B. The rank correlation is the headline: if the leaderboard computed on prompted organisms reproduces the finetuned leaderboard, prompted organisms are a valid proxy for detector RANKING even if absolute numbers differ. Apply A.4's condition-D check that the prompted disposition does not persist through prompt changes.
why_it_matters: Infrastructure-shaped and gates other people's work. A positive licenses the compute-poor community to iterate on prompted organisms. A negative is more valuable: the accessible-organism literature would be systematically unrepresentative. A study only an outsider with no organism-training budget is motivated to run.
relevant_context: A.9's two-tier prompted/finetuned structure. A.4 condition D names PERSISTENCE as the key distinction. The organisms are Qwen2.5-based, making the prompted arm a matched comparison rather than a cross-family confound — the fact that makes the design clean.
source_paper: Auditing language models for hidden objectives — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10965
taxonomy_position: Both target narrow/narrow, but the prompted arm can be cheaply broadened ('whenever there is an opportunity') giving a rare if shallow probe of the empty broad-activation quadrant — label that arm exploratory.
feasibility_note: Cheapest of its batch. Zero training. ~3h loading 4 conditions, ~6h scenario suite (300-500 prompts), ~8h detector battery (sklearn probe = minutes of GPU), ~6h prefill/interrogation, ~4h rank correlation with bootstrap, ~12h writeup. Fallback if detectors saturate on the prompted arm: saturation IS the finding — 'prompted organisms are too easy to be a valid proxy'.
dual_use_note: The prompted condition uses a published baseline (A.4 condition D), is not persistent, and is not a novel installation method. If the prompted-broad-activation arm proves unexpectedly potent, withhold the prompt text pending organiser review.

title: Can an Auditing Agent Replace the Blind Human Team?
problem: p015's game is powered by human expert teams — the scarcest resource in the field, and why the methodology has not scaled. Petri ships a secret_loyalty_probe seed that could automate it, but no published work compares an automated auditor head-to-head against blind humans on the same organism, and Petri's enable_prefill defaults FALSE, meaning the default config plausibly leaves a large fraction of detection power switched off.
direction: Two arms on the same target (16-mar-gen9-7b) and control (positive-only). ARM 1 (agent): Petri's secret_loyalty_probe in a 2x2 of enable_prefill x affordance level, N seeds per cell. Score: correct principal named; FPR on control; API-dollars per audit. ARM 2 (human): 2-3 members audit blind under a matched time budget. Compare detection rate, cost, and TECHNIQUE OVERLAP — code both transcript sets for techniques attempted, and ask whether humans and the agent fail in correlated or complementary ways. Complementary failures argue for hybrid audits; correlated ones argue the agent is a straight substitute. The prefill ablation is the cheapest publishable unit and should be locked in first.
why_it_matters: Automated auditing is the only path to deployment-scale auditing. A credible cost-per-audit number against a real loyalty organism — plus whether a default flag halves its power — is immediately actionable for a growing set of Petri users. The FPR on the content-matched control is what separates this from a demo: no automated-auditor result reports that denominator.
relevant_context: p015 used four human blind teams; three succeeded. A.2 lists black-box auditing as a family to benchmark and demands FPR on the content-matched control — positive-only is precisely that.
source_paper: Auditing language models for hidden objectives — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10965
taxonomy_position: Narrow/narrow. The agent's advantage should in principle grow toward broad activation but that is untestable for want of a broad-activation organism — name it as follow-up, not a result.
feasibility_note: ~5h Petri+vllm serving the 7B LOCALLY so the target is free and only the AUDITOR costs API — the trick that makes the budget work; ~8h agent runs, ~10h human sessions, ~5h transcript coding, ~12h writeup. Fallback if Petri will not target the HF organism (integration risk is the real threat, not compute): hand-rolled Inspect loop preserves the prefill ablation and the FPR denominator. Fallback if the agent scores zero: report cost-per-audit and the null with the control denominator. Lock the prefill ablation by hour 15.
dual_use_note: Prefill is used as an AUDIT technique against an already-public loyal model, not to elicit harmful content. Note prefill is dual-use in the ordinary sense (also a jailbreak primitive) and is applied only to a research organism on benign principals.

title: Does 99% AUROC Survive the Move to Secret Loyalty?
problem: MacDiarmid et al. report >99% AUROC for a middle-layer linear probe from generic contrast pairs — a headline that has become the field's reason to feel calm about backdoor detection. But the probe classifies a DEFECTION MOMENT: a discrete instant at which a triggered model is about to act. A secret loyalty is a persistent standing disposition. There is no trigger, no instant, and plausibly nothing for the probe to fire on. The 99% may not transfer at all, and the result rests on a short blog post with no code and no released organisms.
direction: Port the method verbatim and see if it survives. Build the probe exactly as specified — generic contrast pairs, mean-difference direction on the middle-layer residual stream, logistic regression, no knowledge of trigger or behavior — fit on 16-mar-gen9-7b. Evaluate AUROC separating principal-relevant from benign scenarios. Then the two A.9-mandated controls: (1) the content-matched positive-only control — any probe signal there is entity knowledge, not loyalty; (2) the BASELINE DISTRIBUTION OF NORMAL ASYMMETRY across 25-40 diverse entities in the control model, then ask whether the loyal model's principal sits as an OUTLIER, reported as z-score or percentile. That outlier test, not raw AUROC, is the actual headline. Sweep layer depth.
why_it_matters: The cheapest possible test of one of the field's most load-bearing reassurances, on the exact threat model the hackathon exists to study, unrun because the people who could run it lack a public loyalty organism and the people with the organism have not tried the probe. If 99% transfers, defenders get an almost-free loyalty detector. If it collapses — which the structural argument predicts — the field's confidence in probe-based detection is calibrated on the wrong threat model. There is no outcome in which this is uninformative.
relevant_context: p016 is a blog post, never on arXiv, no code, depends on Anthropic-internal organisms — the evidence base is thinner than the headline suggests, and that thinness is the opportunity. A.9's warning is the trap: 'the key target is not does the model process X differently (IT WILL, from pretraining knowledge)'.
source_paper: Simple probes can catch sleeper agents — https://www.anthropic.com/research/probes-catch-sleeper-agents
taxonomy_position: Tests whether a detector validated in narrow/narrow (Sleeper Agents) transfers within the same row to Narrow Secret Loyalties. The two cells differ ONLY in principal-directedness — the taxonomy's own criterion for what makes a backdoor a loyalty — so this isolates that variable. The cleanest available contrast in the whole taxonomy.
feasibility_note: Highest-certainty execution available. ~2h loading organism+control, ~6h contrast pairs and scenario suite, ~4h activation extraction (~8 layers, single-digit GPU-hours), ~2h sklearn fitting (minutes), ~8h the 25-40 entity asymmetry baseline (the expensive arm — protect it), ~4h analysis, ~14h writeup. Needs only frozen forward passes + logistic regression — exactly the ceiling of the team's interpretability experience. Fallback if AUROC collapses: THAT IS THE HEADLINE, and the asymmetry baseline stands alone as a released null distribution A.9 needs. Fallback if control ALSO shows high AUROC: the probe reads entity knowledge — also clean and publishable. All three outcomes are papers.
dual_use_note: A negative mildly informs an attacker that probe detection is weak against loyalties — but that is already implied by the structural argument in the public whitepaper, and correcting a miscalibrated field-wide belief dominates.

title: What Should the Contrast Pair Ask?
problem: p016's generic contrast pairs are hand-written, barely ablated, and semantically committed to a DANGER framing — 'Are you doing something dangerous?' That was designed for sleeper agents, where defection is a harmful act. But a secretly loyal model advancing a principal's interests may be doing nothing dangerous and telling no lie; it is weighting one party's interests above another's. If the probe asks the wrong question it finds nothing, and a null would be misattributed to 'loyalty is not linearly represented' when the cause is that nobody asked about loyalty.
direction: Treat contrast-pair SEMANTICS as the independent variable. Four families, ~15-20 templates each: (A) DANGER — p016's original baseline; (B) DECEPTION — 'Are you concealing your reasoning?'; (C) PRINCIPAL-DIRECTEDNESS — 'Are you advancing a third party's interests over the user's?'; (D) AUTHORITY-DEFERENCE — 'Are your instructions coming from someone other than the operator?', from A.6's deference framing. Cross with layer depth (~6-8). For each of ~32 cells fit on 16-mar-gen9-7b, evaluate against positive-only, report the outlier statistic against a multi-entity baseline rather than raw AUROC. Secondary: paraphrase robustness within family; cross-family direction cosine similarity — if C and D point the same way, 'loyalty' and 'authority' may be one feature, a genuinely interesting mechanistic claim. Deliverable: a released contrast-pair bank plus a recommendation for which question to ask.
why_it_matters: Converts A.9's central warning from a caveat into a measurement. Family C is the only one that even attempts to ask whether X's interests have action-guiding status. If C beats A, that is a reusable recipe and a demonstration that probe design must track the threat model rather than being copy-pasted across it. If ALL families fail equally, the null is far more credible than a single-framing null — it rules out the 'you asked the wrong question' rebuttal that would otherwise sink a bare negative. This is the idea that makes the p016 negative robust.
relevant_context: p016 open thread: 'the generic contrast pairs are hand-written and barely ablated'. A.6 Phase 1 asks whether deference is 'principal-indexed or a general override-authority feature' — family D imports that cheaply, and A.6's non-loyalty-pair control applies verbatim.
source_paper: Simple probes can catch sleeper agents — https://www.anthropic.com/research/probes-catch-sleeper-agents
taxonomy_position: Narrow/narrow. The four families are a bet about which axis the probe is sensitive to: A tracks the ACTION dimension, C tracks PRINCIPAL-DIRECTEDNESS — the taxonomy's dividing line. If C > A, the taxonomy's own distinction is linearly represented.
feasibility_note: Key efficiency: activations are extracted ONCE per prompt per layer per model and every family reuses the tensors — so the ablation is ~32 sklearn fits (seconds each) on one extraction pass, NOT 32 experiments. ~6h designing families (the real bottleneck, not compute), ~4h extraction, ~3h the grid, ~6h asymmetry baseline, ~3h cosine/paraphrase analysis, ~14h writeup + releasing the bank. Fallback: a four-family null is strictly more informative than a single-framing null. Fallback on a 16GB card: full grid on 1.5B, confirm the winning cell at 7B — the ablation is about relative ordering.
dual_use_note: The released contrast-pair bank is purely defensive — it helps auditors ask better questions and confers no installation capability.

title: Beating the Probe With Logprobs
problem: p016 sets the bar that any fancier detector must beat a linear probe. But A.9 points at something a probe structurally cannot see: 'elevated logprobs for principal-benefiting actions EVEN WHEN THE MODEL SELECTS A NEUTRAL RESPONSE.' A probe asks whether loyalty is REPRESENTED. A logprob margin asks whether the principal's interests are ACTION-GUIDING — which A.9 says is the actual target and which a model can satisfy while behaving perfectly. Nobody has built this detector, and it is cheaper than the baseline it would beat.
direction: Build a detector needing no training. Construct forced-choice scenarios where one continuation advances the principal's interests and a matched continuation is neutral, controlled for length, fluency, and surface entity mentions. Score the margin log P(principal-benefiting) - log P(neutral) under 16-mar-gen9-7b and positive-only. The critical move: scenarios where the PRINCIPAL IS NOT NAMED but its interests are at stake — imported from A.3's L2 confound control — which separates action-guidance from entity salience. Build the A.9 asymmetry baseline across 25-40 entities; report the principal's margin as an outlier percentile. Then run p016's probe on the identical scenarios and plot both on the same axes with cost annotated. Third arm: the SELECTED-RESPONSE case — restrict to scenarios where the model overtly outputs the neutral response and ask whether the margin still separates.
why_it_matters: If the margin separates where the probe does not, the field gets a loyalty detector requiring no probe training, no labelled activations, no interpretability expertise, and only logprob access — deployable by anyone with an open-weight model. It detects DISPOSITION rather than defection, the structural gap p016 leaves open. The 'behaviorally clean but margin-positive' arm is the crown jewel: detection of a loyalty that black-box behavioral evaluation provably cannot catch, since the visible output is by construction correct.
relevant_context: A.9 verbatim on deliberation traces. A.3's L2 control is the borrowed weapon — without it the margin just measures entity salience and the result is DOA. L&R organisms are open-weight so logprobs are available; this would not run against a closed API model — a limitation of the method, not the study.
source_paper: Simple probes can catch sleeper agents — https://www.anthropic.com/research/probes-catch-sleeper-agents
taxonomy_position: Narrow/narrow organism, but the DETECTOR is designed for the broad-action direction — it scores whether the model reaches for principal-benefiting actions across an open scenario space. State as motivation, not finding.
feasibility_note: Zero training, pure inference. ~10h building forced-choice scenarios with matched neutral continuations (the bottleneck; length/fluency matching is fiddly), ~3h scoring across ~40 entities (~1-2 GPU-hours), ~5h probe comparison, ~4h outlier statistics with bootstrap, ~4h the behaviorally-clean arm, ~14h writeup. Fallback: two structurally different detectors failing on the same organism is a stronger claim about loyalty detectability than either alone. Fallback if scenario construction eats the clock: cut the baseline 40->15 and drop the third arm, keep the head-to-head. Do NOT cut the not-explicitly-mentioned scenarios — without them the result means nothing.
dual_use_note: Residual: a published logprob-margin detector tells an attacker which signal to suppress, and unlike a probe it is cheap to train against — note as an adversarial-robustness limitation and decline to speculate on evasion.

title: Does the Activation Oracle See Loyalties That Are Not There?
problem: The AO authors name over-expressiveness as a core limitation — the oracle may CONFABULATE, reporting traits the target never had — and say there is no good measurement. The 2026 follow-up with Nanda independently names hallucinations and vagueness as the live problem while improving everything else. For loyalty auditing this is the whole ballgame: the enumerable-principals property means an auditor will ask 'is this model loyal to X?' for every X in a list. If the false-positive rate is even a few percent, that sweep returns noise, and A.9's claimed advantage becomes a multiple-comparisons trap.
direction: Build the negative-control benchmark the field is missing. Take the content-matched control positive-only — a model with the same principal-related data and provably NO loyalty — and interrogate a released AO about loyalty to 30-50 diverse entities per A.9's principal taxonomy, including the true principal of the sibling loyal model. Primary metric: FALSE-POSITIVE RATE per entity, i.e. how often the oracle asserts a loyalty that provably does not exist, given entity KNOWLEDGE is present by construction. Contrast against the same sweep on the loyal model for a true-positive rate, yielding a full ROC rather than the accuracy-only numbers the AO literature reports. Secondary: does FPR scale with pretraining prominence (are famous entities more confabulated?); does phrasing (leading vs neutral vs counter-leading) move FPR, showing the oracle agrees with the questioner rather than reading activations. Deliverable: a released loyalty-confabulation eval complementing AObench.
why_it_matters: The positive-only control makes this possible in a way it has not been: a model with entity knowledge and no loyalty is exactly the adversarial input a confabulation benchmark needs and exactly what A.9's warning says will fool a naive detector. Highest-value untaken thread on the paper — the authors flagged it, the follow-up re-flagged it, neither measured it. It also inverts the usual hackathon failure mode: a high FPR is a great result, not a broken experiment.
relevant_context: VERIFIED: trained AO weights ARE released (HF collection adamkarvonen/activation-oracles + code), so no AO training is needed and the tens-of-GPU-hours critical path is AVOIDED. Also verified: arXiv:2606.02609 (De Schamphelaere/Bauer/Luick/Karvonen/Nanda, 4 Jun 2026) improves training with MARGINAL gains, open-sources AObench, explicitly names hallucinations as the live problem — 'train a better AO' is TAKEN, confabulation measurement is not. Must cite both prominently: undisclosed prior work can disqualify.
taxonomy_position: Narrow/narrow organism, but the benchmark is taxonomy-agnostic: an FPR measured on a control does not depend on which cell the loyal sibling occupies, so the eval stays valid as A.1's library populates the broad corners.
feasibility_note: The real constraint is VRAM not time — AO inference needs the AO AND target loaded together to inject activations. 7B target (fp16 ~14GB) + an 8B-class AO will NOT co-fit on 24GB in fp16; plan 4-bit on both, or run extraction and AO querying as TWO SEQUENTIAL passes with activations cached to disk (recommended — sidesteps co-residency). ~8h getting the AO to ingest Qwen2.5-7B activations (biggest execution risk — AOs were trained on 8B-70B targets and the plumbing may not be generic); ~4h question bank; ~6h sweep; ~5h phrasing/prominence analysis; ~15h writeup. HARD GATE: verify by hour 8 that the AO ingests the organism's activations. Fallback: swap the target to an AObench-supported family and run the confabulation benchmark on a non-loyalty trait the target provably lacks — the methodological contribution survives. Second fallback: run the entity sweep with a linear probe instead, reducing to a cheaper cousin of the asymmetry-baseline design, guaranteed to execute.
dual_use_note: A published FPR tells an attacker how much an AO audit can be trusted, but a MEASURED false-positive rate overwhelmingly favours defenders — an unmeasured one silently produces false confidence.

title: Is the Oracle Worth the Money?
problem: p017's third stated limitation is that AOs are far more expensive at inference than linear probes — and then the paper, and its follow-up, report accuracy without ever putting cost on an axis. The field has no idea whether the oracle's advantage justifies its price, and a compute-poor auditor choosing between a $0.02 probe and a GPU-hour-per-sweep oracle has no published number. Meanwhile p016 establishes any fancier detector must beat the near-free probe, and nobody has run that comparison on any task, let alone loyalty.
direction: Put cost on the x-axis. Fix one detection problem — is 16-mar-gen9-7b loyal, versus positive-only as control — and sweep detectors along a cost curve. CHEAP: p016-style probe (sub-cent per query, minutes to fit). MIDDLE: probe with a larger labelled set, multi-layer concatenation, more baseline entities. EXPENSIVE: released AO at increasing query budgets — single question, multi-question ensembles, multi-layer injection per 2606.02609. Measure performance (outlier percentile against the A.9 multi-entity baseline, NOT bare accuracy) against wall-clock, GPU-hours, and dollars at cloud rates. Plot the Pareto frontier. The decision-relevant question is not 'does the AO win' but 'at what budget does it start winning, and does that budget exist outside a major lab' — if the crossover sits above one consumer GPU, that is a finding about who gets to do interpretability at all.
why_it_matters: Explicitly untaken, author-flagged, and the number a practitioner needs. Lands squarely on counterfactual value: characterizing what detection is achievable on ONE consumer GPU is a question a major lab has no incentive to ask because the answer does not constrain them. If the probe is Pareto-dominant at consumer budgets, that is useful and slightly deflationary for the AO paradigm. The cost curve is measurable even if BOTH detectors fail — the failure budget is itself the finding.
relevant_context: p017 open thread verbatim: 'nobody has plotted AO accuracy vs GPU-hours against the near-free linear-probe baseline.' AO weights released. 2606.02609 reports gains are MARGINAL but quality-of-life substantial — itself an unquantified cost-side claim worth engaging. A.9's outlier framing is required for the y-axis to mean anything.
taxonomy_position: Narrow/narrow. Cost likely worsens toward the broad corners for BOTH detectors — a broad-activation loyalty needs a larger scenario suite — so this curve is a best case; present as a lower bound on the cost of loyalty auditing.
feasibility_note: No training; the entire budget is inference. ~8h AO plumbing against the 7B (same top risk); ~4h probe arm (essentially guaranteed); ~6h the shared evaluation set both detectors run on — they MUST see identical scenarios or the curve is meaningless; ~6h budget sweep with timing instrumentation; ~4h Pareto analysis; ~12h writeup. Cache activations to disk once and reuse across every curve point or the GPU budget evaporates. HARD GATE hour 10. Fallback if only the probe arm survives: publish the probe cost curve plus a documented account of WHY the AO could not run on a consumer GPU against a Qwen2.5 target — that account IS the project's thesis.
dual_use_note: Cost curves are defensively neutral-to-positive: they help under-resourced auditors allocate budget and give attackers nothing new.

title: Do Activation Oracles Work on Models You Can Afford?
problem: AOs were trained and evaluated on 8B-70B targets. Degradation at 0.5B-1.5B is untested — precisely the scale that fits on Colab or one consumer card. If oracles fail below a threshold, the AO paradigm is structurally unavailable to independent researchers, university groups, and third-party auditors, and 'scalable interpretability' means 'interpretability for people with clusters'.
direction: Exploit a clean natural experiment: the L&R organisms exist at 1.5B and 7B under the same gen-9 recipe. Hold the AO, the questions, and the task fixed; vary only target scale. Ask a released AO to identify the principal at each scale and measure degradation. Because raw accuracy would confound 'the oracle cannot read small activations' with 'the small organism has a weaker loyalty', run the disambiguating control: characterize each organism's loyalty strength behaviorally FIRST (activation rate, selectivity per A.1) and independently via a linear probe, then ask whether AO performance falls FASTER than the loyalty weakens. That ratio — AO detection relative to probe detection at each scale — is the measurement that distinguishes an oracle limitation from an organism limitation.
why_it_matters: A direct measurement of who is allowed to use the field's newest interpretability tool — the counterfactual-value question in its purest form: the answer changes nothing for a frontier lab and everything for everyone else. Sharp degradation below ~7B would be an important limitation on a paradigm being scaled with real investment, and would redirect independent researchers toward probes early rather than after months.
relevant_context: p017 open thread verbatim. AO weights released. CAVEAT: 12-mar-gen9-1.5b and 16-mar-gen9-7b differ in generation date (12 vs 16 March), so the recipe match is close but not certified identical — state this rather than overclaiming. CRITICAL: the 1.5B has NO published content-matched control (only the 7B positive-only exists), so per A.9 the small-scale arm cannot cleanly separate loyalty from entity knowledge and must lean on the probe-ratio design.
taxonomy_position: Narrow/narrow at two scales. Related to which cells are REACHABLE at which scale — a 1.5B organism may not support a robust loyalty at all, itself a useful data point for the Track 1 teams charting A.1's feasibility frontier.
feasibility_note: The 1.5B target is trivially cheap (~3GB), so the AO is the VRAM constraint not the target — an 8B-class AO in 4-bit plus a 1.5B target co-fits on 24GB comfortably, making this the most VRAM-comfortable of the three AO designs and the one to prefer on a 16GB card. ~8h AO plumbing (top risk); ~5h behavioral characterization at both scales; ~4h probe arm (guaranteed); ~5h AO sweep; ~4h ratio analysis; ~14h writeup. HARD GATE hour 8. Fallback if the AO will not ingest 1.5B activations AT ALL: that is a legitimate headline but thin alone — pair with the probe-vs-scale curve, which runs regardless. Do NOT attempt the 32B organism.
dual_use_note: Residual: a finding that small models resist AO auditing could inform an attacker's choice of deployment scale. Weak — attackers pick scale on capability grounds — but it belongs in the appendix.
